lead: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 (Pal-GHK) is a synthetic lipopeptide made of the amino acids glycine, histidine and lysine joined to palmitic acid, used in cosmetic skincare. People apply it in creams and serums to look younger: the aim is firmer skin and softer fine lines through more collagen and other dermal matrix in the skin.[2][8] It is marketed as a collagen-stimulating signal peptide and is one of the two peptides in the branded blend Matrixyl 3000, alongside palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7.[1][2]

The appearance logic is cumulative rather than immediate: a cream or serum containing the peptide is applied daily, the lipid chain is meant to help it cross the skin's outer layers, and the aim is a firmer, smoother surface as the dermis is signalled to renew its matrix.[2][12] Plasma levels of the parent GHK peptide are reported to fall from about 200 ng/ml at age 20 to about 80 ng/ml at age 60, which proponents cite as a reason for topical replacement.[11]

Grokipedia attributes its development to the French ingredient company Sederma around 2000, building on the GHK peptide reported in human plasma in 1973 (this account is from an AI-generated source).[2] Wikipedia's article on GHK-Cu, the copper complex of the same tripeptide, says Loren Pickart isolated it from human plasma albumin in 1973, identified it as glycyl-L-histidyl-L-lysine in 1977, and that research from the late 1980s reported increased collagen synthesis in skin fibroblasts.[11]

Published evidence for wrinkle reduction in people is limited: a 2025 review of topical GHK describes cell studies as supportive and notes that published information on skin permeability and effectiveness of GHK-Cu and Pal-GHK is insufficient.[8] Recent papers are laboratory, permeation and small clinical studies.[1][4][5]

chain: Palmitoyl chain increases fat solubility for skin penetration
GHK signal is proposed to prompt fibroblasts to make collagen and matrix
Firmer-looking skin and softer fine lines, as users hope
angle.text: People use serums and creams with palmitoyl tripeptide-1 hoping to firm skin and soften wrinkles. The proposed route is a signalling one: the peptide is meant to tell dermal fibroblasts to produce more collagen and matrix, and the palmitoyl tail is meant to help it into the skin.

paras: The palmitic acid chain, a saturated 16-carbon fatty acid, is attached to the N-terminal glycine of the GHK tripeptide to increase fat solubility and skin penetration.[2] The compound is commonly supplied as a white powder, used in creams and serums, and is described as stable across a mildly acidic to neutral pH range.[2] It is made by standard solid-phase peptide synthesis.[2]

The Matrixyl name was launched in 2000 by the French cosmetic ingredient company Sederma, for a different peptide: palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (Pal-KTTKS), a five-amino-acid chain joined to a 16-carbon fatty chain.[12] Wikipedia notes that this ingredient was called palmitoyl pentapeptide-3 before 2006.[12] Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a separate, later ingredient from the same product lineage, and is paired with palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 in the Matrixyl 3000 blend.[2]

Both belong to a class called matrikines or signal peptides: short fragments modelled on pieces of matrix proteins that, according to the cosmetic-science account, bind receptors and switch on genes involved in renewing the extracellular matrix and in cell proliferation.[12] The fatty chain is meant to help the molecule pass through the skin's lipid layers.[12] Wikipedia cites in vitro and in vivo studies of the pentapeptide, published by Sederma and by independent groups, that report anti-wrinkle effects, and the same article flags the mechanism statement as needing further medical citation.[12]

Wikipedia gives the sequence of Matrixyl itself as Pal-Lys-Thr-Thr-Lys-Ser and cites a 2013 fibroblast collagen study, a 2005 study of topical use on photoaged facial skin and a 2014 skin permeation and stability study among the published work on that pentapeptide.[12] For GHK, Loren Pickart's 1973 isolation was linked to experiments in which older liver cells behaved more like younger ones in younger donors' blood; the active factor was identified as GHK in 1977, and in 1980 it was proposed that GHK-Cu helps move copper into cells.[11]

Manufacturers and reviews describe signal peptides as mimicking collagen breakdown fragments to prompt fibroblasts to make extracellular matrix.[2] A 2025 review states that cell studies leave little doubt that GHK has anti-wrinkle potential, through raising collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis and supporting angiogenesis and nerve outgrowth, but asks whether skin permeability allows it to act at its site of action.[8]

A 2026 study examined circadian rhythm of collagen metabolism in skin fibroblasts and reported opposing day and night phases, then tested palmitoyl tripeptide-1 at night alongside baicalin by day in fibroblasts, in an eight-week mouse study and in a trial in 30 women.[5] A 2026 computational study screened cosmetic peptides for effects on type III collagen using knowledge-graph and docking methods, followed by fibroblast and ex vivo skin tests.[4]

In laboratory and animal work on the copper complex GHK-Cu, effects reported include collagen and glycosaminoglycan synthesis, decorin production, anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions and release of growth factors; the same account notes it stimulates both matrix metalloproteinases and their inhibitors, and that much of the gene-modulation work comes from one research group, with limited human evidence.[11] Wound-healing data are mostly from rabbits, rats, mice and pigs, and no human wound-healing trials are described.[11]

In a 2026 study, serums containing palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 were applied to the skin of three volunteers and the stratum corneum analysed with secondary-ion mass spectrometry; both peptides were detected in all layers with signal falling by depth, suggesting they remained largely between cells.[1]

A 2026 study in European Journal of Pharmacology tested a combination of EGCG, biotin and Pal-GHK in a mouse model of stress-induced alopecia and reported effects on TGF-beta and BMP signalling.[9] A 2025 cell study examined a palmitoyl copper peptide combined with acetyl tyrosine and melanin production in melanoma cell lines.[10]

No randomized trial of palmitoyl tripeptide-1 alone for wrinkles was found. Related work includes the circadian-timed regimen paired with baicalin that included a clinical trial in 30 female participants, a registered trial of an AI-personalized skincare regimen for facial photoaging in 43 women that is not specific to this peptide, and the permeation study in three volunteers.[1][5][6] Wikipedia describes several controlled facial studies of the related GHK-Cu reporting firming and anti-wrinkle effects but notes small samples and short durations.[11]

Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is listed as an ingredient in many serums and creams. US product labels list it in body creams, for example one regimen advising use of a cream three times a day, with warnings for external use only, not on irritated skin, and to discontinue if irritation occurs.[7] The related GHK-Cu is also widely discussed in cosmetics and hair-loss products.[11]
The GHK peptide family is also discussed in connection with the copper complex GHK-Cu, whose research literature is larger.[11]

Copper tripeptide-1 is the INCI name used on products for anti-ageing and hair-loss prevention, and the encyclopedia entry cites several controlled facial studies of GHK-Cu reporting firming and anti-wrinkle effects, with small samples and short durations and a need for further research.[11] Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 itself is listed alongside palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 in many blended serums, so consumer results are usually attributable to the combination.[2]

timeline.event: GHK isolated from human plasma by Loren Pickart.[11]
Sederma launches Matrixyl, patents around this time (reported by Grokipedia).[2]

name: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1

card.summary: The collagen-signal peptide half of Matrixyl 3000; widely used, with mostly lab and permeation data behind it.
card.note: Origin story comes largely from an AI-generated reference; human efficacy trials are sparse.

quick.overview:
Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a lab-made peptide (glycine-histidine-lysine plus a fatty acid) used in anti-wrinkle creams and serums. It is one of the two peptides in Matrixyl 3000.

Recent published work is mostly laboratory, permeation and computational studies; no dedicated wrinkle trial was found.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a signal peptide that prompts skin fibroblasts to make collagen and matrix. The fatty acid chain is meant to help it cross the skin barrier, though one study found the peptides stayed in the outer layer.
quick.risks: Product labels advise external use only, avoiding eyes, and stopping if irritation occurs. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient.
